Surah 89: Al-Fajr

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the dawn.﴾ He swears by the dawn, which is the morning (ṣubḥ), like His saying: ﴿And by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34], or by the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-fajr).

And by ten nights (﴿وَلَيالٍ عَشْرٍ﴾), the ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah, or the first ten nights of Muharram, or the last ten nights of Ramadan. They are indefinite (nukkirat) only to increase their excellence.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 3:

﴿By the even and the odd﴾, the even of all things and their odd, or the even and odd of these nights, or the even and odd of the prayer, or the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), because it is the tenth day, and the Day of 'Arafah, because it is the ninth, or the creation and the Creator. "Wa'l-witr" (the odd), [read with a kasra] by Hamzah and 'Ali, and with a fatha on the waw by others. These are two dialects: the fatha is Hijazi and the kasra is Tamimi. After swearing by the specific nights, he swore by nights in general, so he said:

﴿By the night﴾, and it is said: what is meant is the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr),

﴿when it passes on﴾, i.e., when it goes away. The yā' of "yasri" is dropped in continuous speech (al-darj), being replaced by the kasra. A man asked al-Akhfash about the dropping of the yā', and he said: "No, not until you serve me for a year." So he asked him after a year, and he said: "The night does not travel (yasri); rather, travelling occurs in it (yusra fihi)." (p-638) Since he deviated from its meaning, he deviated from its wording, for the sake of concordance. It is also said: the meaning of "yasri" is: travelled in it (yusra fihi), just as one says "a sleeping night" (laylun na'im), meaning: one sleeps in it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 5:

﴿Is there in that﴾ i.e., in what I have sworn by, of these things,

﴿an oath﴾ i.e., a thing sworn by,

﴿for one of intellect (dhī ḥijr)﴾, meaning one of reason ('aql). It is called ḥijr because it restrains (yaḥjur) from recklessness in what is not fitting, just as it is called "'aql" and "nuhyah," because it comprehends ('aqala) and restrains (yanhā). The meaning is: Is it fitting in his estimation that it be magnified by swearing by them? Or: is there in my swearing by them an oath for one of intellect? That is: is it a great oath, by the like of which the sworn-about matter is affirmed? Or: is there in swearing by these things a convincing oath for one who has reason and understanding? The sworn-about matter is omitted, and it is His saying: "Surely He will punish" (la-yu'adhdhibanna), which is indicated by His saying: "Have you not seen" down to His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 13]. Then He mentioned the punishment of the nations that denied the Messengers, and said:

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, [the people of] Iram of the pillars?﴾ That is, "Did you not know, O Muhammad, with a knowledge that equals direct observation in certainty?" It is a rhetorical question meant to affirm. It is said that ʿĀd was the name of the descendants of ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūh, just as Hāshim is used for the Banū Hāshim. The earliest of them were called ʿĀd al-Ūlā (the First ʿĀd) and Iram, naming them after their grandfather, while those who came after them were called ʿĀd al-Ākhira (the Last ʿĀd). So "Iram" is in apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "ʿĀd," and it indicates that they are the First ʿĀd, the ancient ones. It is also said that "Iram" is their city and the land in which they lived. This is supported by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr, "bi-ʿādi Iram," in the genitive construction, with the implied meaning "by ʿĀd, the people of Iram," like the words of Allah, ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yūsuf 12:82]. It is not declined (lam tanṣarif), whether it is a tribe or a land, because of definiteness and feminine form. As for "dhāt al-ʿimād" (possessing pillars): if it is an attribute of the tribe, the meaning is that they were nomads, people of tent-poles, or men of tall bodies, comparing their statures to pillars. If it is an attribute of the city, the meaning is that it had many columns. It is narrated that ʿĀd had two sons, Shaddād and Shadīd. They ruled and prevailed, then Shadīd died, and the affair passed entirely to Shaddād, who ruled the world, and its kings submitted to him. He heard the mention of Paradise and said, "I will build something like it." So he built Iram in the desert of ʿAdan (Aden), over three hundred years, while his lifespan was nine hundred years. It was a great city whose palaces were of gold and silver, and whose columns were of chrysolite and ruby, and in it were all kinds of trees and rivers. When its construction was completed [p. 639], he set out toward it with the people of his kingdom. When he was one day and one night's journey away from it, Allah sent upon them a cry from the sky, and they all perished. It is related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qilāba on the authority of [others] that he went out seeking his camels and came upon it, and he carried away whatever he could of what was there. News of this reached Muʿāwiya, who summoned him and he recounted the story to him. Muʿāwiya then sent for Kaʿb, and asked him. Kaʿb said, "It is Iram of the pillars, and a man from the Muslims will enter it in your time, reddish-white, short, with a mole on his eyebrow and a mole on his heel, who will go out seeking his camels." Then he turned and saw Ibn Qilāba, and said, "By Allah, this is that man."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 8:

﴿The like of which had not been created in the lands﴾. That is: the like of [the people of] 'Ad, in their strength and the height of their stature. The height of a man among them was four hundred cubits (dhira'). Or: there had not been created the like of the city of Shaddad in all the lands of the world.

Thamud, who hewed the rock (﴿وَثَمُودَ الَّذِينَ جابُوا الصَخْرَ﴾), cut out the rocks of the mountains and took dwellings for themselves in them. It was said: the first to hew mountains and rocks were the Thamud, and they built one thousand and seven hundred cities, all of them of stone.

﴿بِالوادِ﴾: in the Wadi (valley), namely Wadi al-Qura.

And Pharaoh, owner of the stakes (﴿وَفِرْعَوْنَ ذِي الأوْتادِ﴾). That is, owner of many troops, for they had many tent-pegs (maḍārib) which they drove in whenever they camped. It was also said: he had stakes with which he used to torture people, as he did to Āsiyah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 11:

﴿Alladhina﴾ (who), in the accusative case, by way of censure (dhamm), or in the nominative case, as in "they are those who" (hum alladhina), or in the genitive case, as a description of those mentioned: "ʿAd, Thamud and Fir'awn" — ﴿tagha fi al-bilad﴾ (they transgressed in the lands), meaning they exceeded the limit.
﴿Therefore they multiplied corruption therein﴾, through disbelief, killing, and oppression.

(p-640) ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. This is a metaphor for inflicting the punishment upon them in the most emphatic manner, since "pouring" (ṣabb) conveys continuity, and "scourge" (sawṭ) conveys increased pain. That is: they were punished with a painful punishment that was continuous.

Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful (﴿إنَّ رَبَّكَ لَبِالمِرْصادِ﴾). The mirṣād (مِرْصاد) is the place where one lies in wait and keeps watch; it is of the pattern mifʿāl, derived from "raṣadahu" (he watched him, lay in ambush for him). This is an image (mathal) for His watching over His servants, that they cannot escape Him, that He knows what proceeds from them, and that He preserves it, and so He will recompense them for it: if it is good, then good, and if it is evil, then evil.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verses 15–16:**

﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him, honoring him and bestowing blessings upon him, he says, "My Lord has honored me."﴾ ﴿But when He tests him by restricting his provision for him,﴾ i.e., He constricted it for him and made it only sufficient for his subsistence. "*Faqaddara*" (with the doubled *dal*) is read by al-Shāmī and Yazīd.

﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ i.e., it is incumbent upon one whose Lord is watchful over him (*bi-l-mirṣād*) to strive for the outcome (*al-ʿāqibah*) and not to be concerned with the immediate life (*al-ʿājilah*). But he has reversed this. When his Lord tests him with blessing and abundance, so that he would give thanks, he says, "My Lord has honored me," meaning He has favored me with what He gave me. So he sees honor in an abundance of worldly fortune. And when He tests him with poverty, restricting his provision so that he would be patient, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me," so he sees humiliation in a scarcity of worldly fortune, because he is concerned only with the immediate life and what delights and pleases him therein. So He refuted his claim with His saying:

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verses 15–16:**

﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him, honoring him and bestowing blessings upon him, he says, "My Lord has honored me."﴾ ﴿But when He tests him by restricting his provision for him,﴾ i.e., He constricted it for him and made it only sufficient for his subsistence. "*Faqaddara*" (with the doubled *dal*) is read by al-Shāmī and Yazīd.

﴿Then he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ i.e., it is incumbent upon one whose Lord is watchful over him (*bi-l-mirṣād*) to strive for the outcome (*al-ʿāqibah*) and not to be concerned with the immediate life (*al-ʿājilah*). But he has reversed this. When his Lord tests him with blessing and abundance, so that he would give thanks, he says, "My Lord has honored me," meaning He has favored me with what He gave me. So he sees honor in an abundance of worldly fortune. And when He tests him with poverty, restricting his provision so that he would be patient, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me," so he sees humiliation in a scarcity of worldly fortune, because he is concerned only with the immediate life and what delights and pleases him therein. So He refuted his claim with His saying:

﴿Kallā﴾ (ﷻ) means: wealth is not what makes one honoured or humiliated, whether it is abundant or scarce. Rather, honour lies in being granted success in obedience, and humiliation lies in being forsaken.

His (ﷻ) saying "fa-yaqūlu" (then he says) is the predicate (khabar) of the mubtada' (subject), which is "al-insān" (the human being). The entry of the particle "fa" (فَ) is due to the meaning of the conditional (shart) contained in "amma" (أمّا). The adverbial phrase placed between the subject and the predicate is taken as if it were postponed, as though it were said: "As for the human being, he says, 'My Lord has honoured me,' at the time of trial." Likewise, the second "fa-yaqūlu" is the predicate of an implied subject, whose assumed form is: "And as for him, when his Lord tests him..."

Both matters, the expansion of provision and its restriction, are called a trial (ibtilā'), because each of them is a test of the servant. When He expands provision for him, He has tested his condition: will he give thanks or disbelieve? And when He restricts it for him, He has tested his condition: will he be patient or despair? A similar verse is His (ﷻ) saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 35].

He denied his saying "My Lord has honoured me," although He affirmed it in His saying "then He honours him," because he said it with the intention contrary to what Allah had made correct and affirmed. His intention was that Allah gave him what He gave him as an honour to him, because he deserved it, like His saying: ﴿I was given it only on knowledge that is with me﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 78]. In fact, Allah (ﷻ) gave it to him as a trial, without any merit on his part.

﴿Rather, you do not honour the orphan﴾

"And you do not urge one another to feed the poor." That is: rather, there is worse than this saying, namely that God honors them with wealth, so they do not discharge what is incumbent upon them regarding it, namely honoring the orphan with kindness, and urging his people to feed the poor.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 19:**

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾, that is, the estate (al-mirath),

﴿devouring it greedily﴾, that is, with a mixing together (lamm), which is the combining of the lawful and the unlawful. They would not give inheritance to women or to children, and they would consume their inheritance together with their own inheritance (turath).

﴿And you love wealth﴾, it is said: "ḥabbahu" and "aḥabbahu" have the same meaning.

﴿with intense love﴾: abundantly, greatly, strongly, together with greed and withholding of rights.

"Rabbī" (the reading of Ḥijāzī and Abū ʿAmr).

"Yukrimūna" ("they honour"), "wa-lā yaḥuḍḍūna" ("and they do not urge"), "wa-yakulūna" ("and they devour"), and "wa-yuḥibbūna" ("and they love") are the reading of the Baṣrī school.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 21:

﴿Nay!﴾ A rebuke to them for that, and a denunciation of their act. Then he brought the threat, and mentioned their regret over what they neglected, at a time when regret will not benefit, so he said: ﴿Nay! When the earth is pounded to powder﴾, when it is shaken violently,

﴿pounded to powder, again and again﴾, pounded after pounding; that is, the pounding was repeated upon it, until it became scattered dust (hab'an manthuran).

﴿And your Lord comes﴾, an allegory for the manifestation of the signs of His power and the demonstration of the effects of His dominion and authority. For when a king comes in person, the awe that appears through his presence is greater than what appears through the presence of his soldiers and close attendants alone. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "His command and His decree."

﴿And the angels, rank upon rank﴾, meaning: the angels of each heaven descend and stand in ranks, one rank after another, encircling the jinn and mankind.

﴿And Hell will be brought forth on that Day﴾. It has been said: it will be made manifest to its people, like His words: ﴿And Hellfire will be brought forth for those who go astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 91]. And it has been said: it is to be taken according to its literal reality. Thus in the hadith: "Hell will be brought on that Day, having seventy thousand bridles, with each bridle seventy thousand angels dragging it."

﴿On that Day man will remember﴾, i.e., he will be admonished.

﴿But how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾ And from where would he have the benefit of remembrance?!

"He will say, 'Oh, would that I had sent forth (good deeds) for my life (to come)!'" — this life, that is, the life of the Hereafter. That is, "Oh, would that I had sent forth righteous deeds in this transient life for my everlasting life."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 25:

﴿So on that Day, none will punish as He punishes.﴾ That is: none will take charge of the punishment of Allah, because the command belongs to Allah alone on that Day.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 26:

﴿And none binds⁠ ﴾, with chains and shackles,

﴿His bonds as anyone⁠﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "None punishes anyone as the punishment of God, and none binds anyone as the bonds of God," "لا يُعَذَّبُ" (none is punished), "وَلا يُوثَقُ" (nor is bound), "عَلِيٌّ" (ʿAlī), and this is the recitation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Abu ʿAmr returned to it at the end of his life. The pronoun refers to the human being described, who is the disbeliever. It has been said that he is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, meaning: none is punished like his punishment, and none is bound with chains like his bonds, because of his extremity in disbelief and obstinacy. Then God (Exalted) says to the believer:

﴿O soul﴾, honoring it, as He spoke to Musa (peace be upon him), or it may be on the tongue of an angel,

﴿at peace﴾, secure, which fear and grief cannot unsettle. It is the believing soul, or the soul at rest in the truth, which the snow of certainty has calmed, so doubt does not stir within it. The first interpretation is supported by the recitation of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b, a companion and early Qur'an reciter), which reads: "يا أيَّتُها النَفْسُ الآمِنَةُ المُطْمَئِنَّةُ" ("O soul that is secure and at peace"). It is said to the soul at death, or at resurrection, or at its entry into Paradise:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 28:

﴿Return to﴾ your Lord (ilā rabbiki), i.e., to the promise of your Lord, or the reward of your Lord,

﴿well-pleased﴾ (rāḍiyah), with Allah, with what you were given,

﴿and well-pleasing﴾ (marḍiyyah), in the sight of Allah, because of what you did.
﴿So enter among My servants﴾: into the company of My righteous servants; join their ranks.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 89, verse 30:

﴿Enter among My servants﴾, i.e., among them. Abu 'Ubayda said: "That is, with My servants," and "among My servants" means: My chosen ones (khawass), as in the saying: ﴿And admit me, by Your mercy, among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml: 19]. It has also been said: "al-nafs" here means the spirit (al-ruh), and the meaning is: "Enter into the bodies of My servants," based on the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "into the body of My servant." When Ibn 'Abbas died at al-Ta'if, a bird appeared whose form had not been seen before; it entered his bier. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and no one knew who had recited it. It has been said that it was revealed concerning Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and it has been said that it was revealed concerning Khubayb, whom the people of Makkah crucified. It has also been said that it is general in its application to the believers, since the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion of revelation.
